articles.title: MD5 checksums on Samsung firmware: catching a corrupted download before Odin fails
articles.excerpt: You flashed a firmware file with Odin, it failed halfway through, and now the phone won't boot. The file was from a reputable source and matched your model. What went wrong? In a large share of these…
articles.body: You flashed a firmware file with Odin, it failed halfway through, and now the phone won't boot. The file was from a reputable source and matched your model. What went wrong? In a large share of these cases, the answer is embarrassingly simple: the download was corrupted, and nobody checked. Firmware files are big — several gigabytes — and big downloads break silently. A few flipped bits in a multi-gigabyte ZIP don't make it fail to open; they make Odin choke at 40% of the flash with a cryptic error, leaving your phone in an unbootable state. The fix takes ten seconds and almost nobody does it: verify the checksum. What a checksum actually is. A checksum (usually MD5 for Samsung firmware) is a short fingerprint computed from the file's exact contents.

articles.body: Teaching Morse code sounds old-fashioned until you see what it does to a classroom. Dots and dashes give pupils a hands-on reason to practise spelling, rhythm, sequencing and teamwork — no batteries required. Here are five activities that genuinely work, ordered from easiest to most ambitious. 1. Flashlight sentences Darken the classroom and let pupils send each other short words with a torch: long flashes for dashes, short flashes for dots. Start with names. Keep a free morse code alphabet chart open on the projector so the letter patterns stay visible while they work. 2. Clap-back decoding You clap (or tap the desk) a letter; the class writes it down. Speed up gradually. This trains pure listening and doubles as a great five-minute warm-up before English or music lessons. 3.

articles.body: Europe has dropped the ball on the prototype for its first reusable spacecraft. Or, rather, the prototype itself was dropped — on purpose — but the outcome of its fall was not what engineers had hoped for. The incident occurred during an Oct. 6 drop test of the full-scale Space Rider model , from the European Space Agency (ESA). The robotic vehicle's initial drogue parachute deployed successfully, but its main parafoil detached during deployment, leaving the prototype unable to slow its descent before crashing into the ground, according to ESA officials. The cause of the failure remains under investigation.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 22, 1992: Ashes of 'Star Trek' creator Gene Roddenberry launch into space on NASA shuttle
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 22, 1992, the space shuttle Columbia launched into space with the ashes of Gene Roddenberry, the creator of "Star Trek." Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 22, 1992, the space shuttle Columbia launched into space with the ashes of Gene Roddenberry, the creator of " Star Trek ," aboard. During mission STS-52, NASA astronaut and shuttle commander James Wetherbee brought a small container with a portion of Roddenberry's ashes into space as part of his personal effects at the request of Roddenberry's widow, Majel Barrett . It was Roddenberry's lifelong dream to go to space, but he never got to go while he was alive. But thanks to his wife, a little bit of Roddenberry finally made it to space almost exactly one year after his death. NASA and his family didn't tell anyone about it until almost two years later in 1994. Wetherbee said he was "honored to be asked" by Barrett to carry Roddenberry's ashses on the spaceflight.
